title: Nor'easter Slams Northeast, Flooding Streets and Grounding Flights
summary:
Tens of millions of people across the northeastern U.S. woke up Saturday to flooded streets, cancelled flights, and dark homes as a powerful nor'easter — a storm that forms along the East Coast and brings winds from the northeast — pounded the region from Virginia to Maine.

In New Jersey, coastal towns like Surf City and Manasquan saw streets and homes swallowed by floodwater. In Beach Haven West, residents paddled through their neighborhood in kayaks. More than 100,000 households lost electricity, according to the tracker PowerOutage. Air travel was chaotic: more than 2,400 flights were delayed and another 1,199 were grounded, FlightAware reported. The Federal Aviation Administration urged passengers to check with their airlines.

Both New York and New Jersey declared states of emergency. "I urge all New Jerseyans to take this storm seriously, stay alert and follow local guidance," Governor Mikie Sherrill said. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani told residents in a video message: "Don't travel if you don't have to. Do not drive or walk through floodwater."

The National Weather Service warned of "dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds and heavy rainfall." In its alert, the NWS told people to "prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses." Saturday's full moon made things worse by pulling the ocean higher than usual, which is expected to worsen coastal flooding.

Sports and entertainment didn't escape either. The Boston Red Sox moved their final game against the Chicago Cubs to Sunday afternoon in Florida. A professional soccer match between Red Bull New York and St Louis City SC was cancelled. The Global Citizen Festival in Central Park — which was to feature Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean, and John Legend — was called off, and Ed Sheeran's concert at Gillette Stadium near Boston was cancelled for safety reasons.

Forecasters say the storm will continue to bring rain and strong winds through the weekend, with residents urged to stay off the roads and away from floodwaters.
why_it_matters: Storms like this decide whether kids get to school, whether families keep power and water, and how much cities spend on sea walls, drainage and buried power lines — choices that will shape how livable coastal towns are for today's students when they grow up.

background_read: Nor'easters are a regular pattern on the U.S. East Coast: cold air from the north crashes into warmer ocean air, and the spinning storm shoves seawater toward the shore.

The National Weather Service (the U.S. government agency that issues weather forecasts and warnings) uses the word 'inundation' for water rising over land that is normally dry, which is why its alerts tell people to prepare 'immediately.'
Coastal flooding gets much worse when a full moon lines up with the sun, because their combined pull creates the highest tides of the month, sometimes called 'king tides.'
The region has lived through this before — Hurricane Sandy's storm surge flooded large parts of New York and New Jersey, and led to years of rebuilding and new flood protections.
The Federal Aviation Administration (the agency that runs U.S. air traffic control) grounds flights when strong winds and poor visibility make flying unsafe.

perspectives.perspective: Positive: the warnings and shutdowns worked
perspectives.description: Forecasters and officials gave loud, early alerts, declared states of emergency and pulled people off the roads. Cancelling games and concerts and moving a baseball game kept tens of thousands of people out of dangerous places.

perspectives.perspective: Critical: the region keeps flooding in the same places
perspectives.description: The towns hit hardest are the same low-lying communities that flood again and again, and power fails quickly across a huge area. Critics say not enough has been spent on drainage, raised homes and stronger grids.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral/analytical: a normal weather pattern with bigger consequences
perspectives.description: Nor'easters are nothing new on the East Coast. What has changed is how much is built near the water, so the same storm now floods more streets, more basements and more businesses than it would have decades ago.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking: what cities and residents do next
perspectives.description: The next questions are practical — whether coastal towns build higher sea defenses, whether utilities bury power lines, and whether families change where they live and how they travel as these storms keep arriving.
